It's affable entertainment with many funny moments, but not enough to disguise the mechanical structure and whiff of moldiness of its infidelity-interruptus plot.
Yet despite all this frantic activity, this Roundabout show is a slog.
Emerging from “Don’t Dress for Dinner” after the last clandestine smooch had been snatched and the last bedroom door slammed, I found myself itchy with irritation, checking my skin for hives.
It's tired, warmed-over farce that involves seltzer spraying, imaginary insects, boob jokes, loads of alcohol, people jumping over sofas, and the cast running around in dressing gowns.
You mainly wait for this busy, bland meal to end, so you can get dessert someplace else.
BOTTOM LINE Lame sex farce badly done
It’s nearer to Applebee’s than Per Se.
While the mayhem in Don't Dress for Dinner never rises to the dizzying heights of Boeing
I found 'Don't Dress for Dinner' to be head-knockingly convoluted.
Except for a few visual gags, William Ivey Long's divine costumes and the delightfully quirky Kayden, don't expect any such magic from John Tillinger's dull pedestrian production.
If the whole company had followed Kayden's lead, or if director John Tillinger had revved up his tepid staging, this could have been a satisfying 'Dinner.'
There are few things in the theater more distressing than a labored farce.
